evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: All clinician-survey percentages in this document (e.g., wait-time, diagnostic-delay-reason, insurance-barrier, stigma, and regulatory-investigation percentages from the n=155 clinician survey, and the cited background patient-survey percentages) are reported as single pooled national figures with no breakdown by patient or clinician sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: Clinicians report that inadequate physician education about tick-borne disease is the leading cited reason for diagnostic delay (86%), that no reliable diagnostic test exists to confirm ongoing infection or cure, and that the insurance reimbursement model does not accommodate the time/complexity PLD/CLD care requires, producing a structural supply/demand gap, widespread insurance-network non-participation, and professional marginalization (stigma, medical board/insurer investigations) of treating clinicians.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Results sections 3.2-3.3 and Discussion, Healthcare 2022, 10, 1882, pp.4-7.

## Source
Johnson & Maloney (2022), *Healthcare* 10, 1882: a survey of 155 self-selected U.S. clinicians treating persistent/chronic Lyme disease (PLD/CLD), recruited via LymeDisease.org's clinician network and broader email outreach, conducted September-December 2021 across 30 states.

## What the inputs represent
All percentage inputs (wait times, out-of-state patient share, diagnostic-delay reasons, insurance-network non-participation, prior-authorization burden, regulatory/medical-board investigation exposure) are clinician-reported perceptions from this single survey, not direct patient-level measurements and not a representative sample of U.S. clinicians generally. The one dollar figure (annual out-of-pocket cost, $10,000-$20,000) comes from a single respondent's open-text comment, not an aggregated survey statistic; the document contains no other direct-cost or indirect-cost figures.

## Limitations
The pooled percentages in this document (wait-time, diagnostic-delay-reason, insurance-barrier, and investigation-exposure figures) have not been checked for variation by clinician or patient sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or similar subgroup characteristics; federal survey data sources (e.g., MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally support disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform one.

The document also documents a systemic gap distinct from the accuracy or funding of any burden estimate: clinicians report that inadequate physician education about tick-borne disease is the leading cited reason for diagnostic delay (86%), that no reliable diagnostic test exists to confirm ongoing infection or cure, and that the insurance reimbursement model does not accommodate the time and complexity PLD/CLD care requires - together producing a structural supply/demand gap, widespread insurance-network non-participation, and professional marginalization (stigma, medical-board/insurer investigations) of treating clinicians.

The clinician sample is self-selected and non-random, which the authors themselves note limits generalizability of every percentage reported. No patient-level demographic breakdown, aggregate cost totals, or indirect-cost (lost income, caregiving time) figures appear anywhere in this document. The diagnostic-delay-reason comparison in this simulator reflects only how often clinicians cited each reason in this sample; it does not establish which cause is objectively more common or more severe for any individual patient.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Estimated new Lyme disease diagnoses per year, US (cited from Kugeler et al. 2021) (2010-2018 average, the United States): the document's estimate of 476,000 is 13.6 times the 34,973 cases CDC received as reported (yearly totals ranged 30,158 to 42,743). Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
